passages.t: Azariah, a good king in a separate house
passages.happening:
In the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam, Azariah son of Amaziah becomes king of Judah at sixteen and reigns fifty-two years in Jerusalem (verses 1-2). He does what is right, as his father did, though the high places remain (verses 3-4).

‘And the LORD afflicted the king with leprosy until the day he died, so that he lived in a separate house while his son Jotham had charge of the palace and governed the people of the land’ (verse 5). Azariah dies and is buried in the City of David, and Jotham reigns (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Azariah is also called Uzziah. He reigned about 792 to 740 BC, at first beside his father and at the end beside his son, and the reckoning of those overlaps is debated. Isaiah dates his call to the year King Uzziah died.

His disease was what the law called tsara'at, a term for a range of skin diseases, not only what medicine now calls Hansen's disease. It made a person unclean and required living apart, which is why the king lived in a separate house and could not enter the temple. The text says the LORD afflicted him. Chronicles explains further that it came after Uzziah, grown powerful and proud, went into the temple to burn incense, a task kept for the priests.
passages.later: Isaiah wrote, ‘In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord seated on a throne, high and exalted’ (Isaiah 6:1). Chronicles says that ‘when Uzziah grew powerful, his arrogance led to his own destruction’ (2 Chronicles 26:16).
passages.hard:
Was the king's illness a punishment, and what does that mean for anyone who is ill?

The text says the LORD afflicted the king, and Chronicles ties it to a particular act of pride in the temple. That is what the Bible says about one king at one moment. It is not a rule for reading anyone else's illness. Azariah did right, the chapter says, and still lived his last years apart, and the book records it without making him a warning to the sick.

It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul prayed and was not healed, and no one blames him. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Azariah was a good king who ended his days set apart. Ask how you hold together faithfulness and suffering. And ask who in your life lives in a separate house, set apart by illness, and how you might reach them.

passages.t: Five kings in Samaria, and Assyria at the door
passages.happening:
Zechariah son of Jeroboam reigns six months in Samaria and does evil (verses 8-9). Shallum son of Jabesh conspires against him and kills him in front of the people (verse 10). ‘So the word of the LORD spoken to Jehu was fulfilled’ (verse 12): four generations of his sons had sat on the throne.

Shallum reigns one month. Menahem son of Gadi comes up from Tirzah, kills him and reigns in his place (verses 13-14). When the town of Tiphsah will not open its gates, Menahem attacks it with terrible cruelty, sparing not even pregnant women (verse 16). He reigns ten years and does evil (verses 17-18). Pul king of Assyria invades, and Menahem pays him a thousand talents of silver ‘in order to gain his support and strengthen his own grip on the kingdom’ (verse 19). He raises it by taking fifty shekels from each of the wealthy men of Israel, and the king of Assyria withdraws (verse 20).

Menahem's son Pekahiah reigns two years, until his officer Pekah son of Remaliah, with fifty men of Gilead, kills him in the citadel of the palace (verses 23-25). Pekah reigns and does evil (verses 27-28). ‘In the days of Pekah king of Israel, Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came’ (verse 29) and takes town after town in the north, with Gilead and Galilee and all the land of Naphtali, ‘and he took the people as captives to Assyria’ (verse 29). Then Hoshea son of Elah conspires against Pekah, kills him and reigns in his place (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 14 ended at a high tide of northern prosperity. Here the tide goes out. Within a few years of Jeroboam's death Israel has six months of one king, one month of another, a civil war and an empire at the door. The word to Jehu is fulfilled and then spent.

This is the most compressed chapter of royal formulas in Kings, seven reigns in thirty-eight verses, and the formulas become the message. The same verdict falls on every northern king, and the same turning from Jeroboam's sins is never taken. The verb conspire, qashar, literally to tie or bind together, comes again and again: a kingdom tying itself in knots of plot and counterplot.

The decisive figure outside is Tiglath-pileser III, who ruled Assyria from 745 to 727 BC and turned it into an empire that swallowed its neighbors rather than raiding them. The Bible calls him Pul, a name Babylonian records also used. His own inscriptions list Menahem of Samaria among the kings who paid him tribute, usually dated around 738 BC. A thousand talents at fifty shekels a head means Menahem taxed about sixty thousand landowners. Tribute protected a ruler while it drained his people.

In about 733 to 732 BC Tiglath-pileser campaigned against Damascus and Israel, took Galilee and the land east of the Jordan, and deported their people. His inscriptions also claim that the Israelites overthrew Pekah and that he set Hoshea on the throne. Excavations at Hazor found a thick destruction layer from this time. The word for carrying into exile, galah, appears here for the first time of Israelites taken to Assyria. Pekah's twenty years are hard to fit, and many scholars think he first ruled as a rival king in Gilead.
passages.later: Hosea, preaching in these years, said for the LORD, ‘They set up kings, but not by Me’ (Hosea 8:4). Isaiah promised the very lands taken first: ‘In the past He humbled the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the future He will honor the Way of the Sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations’ (Isaiah 9:1). Matthew quotes that promise when Jesus begins his work in Galilee (Matthew 4:15-16).
passages.hard:
Why does the chapter report Menahem's cruelty at Tiphsah without condemning it?

Kings often tells terrible deeds without comment, and some readers take this as indifference. But the book works by building up a picture. Menahem receives the standard verdict that he did evil in the sight of the LORD, and his reign sits in a chapter whose whole message is that the northern kingdom is collapsing under its own violence. The prophets of the same generation say plainly what the narrator implies. Amos names this very crime as a reason for God's judgment on Ammon, and Hosea speaks of Samaria's end in similar terms.

Describing is not approving. The Bible records the worst of what its own people did, which is part of why its account can be trusted. It names the act in one line and leaves the reader to feel it, and these notes do not add to it. The silence is not neutrality. It is the silence of a narrator who expects the reader to know what God thinks of such things.
passages.asks: Menahem paid a heavy price to secure his own position, and his people paid it for him. Ask where you see leaders protect themselves at the cost of those they serve. And ask where you have done the same on a smaller scale.

passages.happening:
In the second year of Pekah, Jotham son of Uzziah becomes king of Judah at twenty-five and reigns sixteen years in Jerusalem (verses 32-33). He does what is right, as his father did. The high places remain, and Jotham rebuilds the Upper Gate of the house of the LORD (verses 34-35).

‘In those days the LORD began to send Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah against Judah’ (verse 37). Jotham dies and is buried in the City of David, and his son Ahaz reigns (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
Judah's two long and fairly stable reigns frame the rapid collapse in the north, and the contrast is sharp. Jotham governed for his father during his illness, about 750 BC, and reigned alone from about 740 BC. Isaiah, Hosea and Micah were preaching in his days.

Verse 37 is set apart as an aside that looks ahead. It opens the crisis of the next chapter, when Aram and Israel march on Jerusalem. Even the hostile moves of foreign kings are described as under God's direction, without excusing those kings for their own aims.
passages.later: Micah dates his preaching to ‘the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah’ (Micah 1:1), and Isaiah dates his visions to the same kings, with Uzziah before them (Isaiah 1:1).
passages.asks: Jotham did right and still left the high places standing. Ask what you have left in place because everyone around you has always kept it. And ask what trouble may be gathering at your borders while life seems calm.
